tooltip.semiconductor-lab.route.sulfate: Route: sulfuric acid, not distilled (up to 9N)
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note: Natural graphite from metamorphic rock (e.g. Sri Lanka vein graphite). Same stuff as pencil lead.
block.semiconductor-lab.magnetite_ore.no: Fe3O4, the natural magnet (lodestone). Found deep in ancient banded iron formations.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note: Magnetite grains washed out of rock and concentrated on beaches. Japanese tatara steel was made from this.
block.semiconductor-lab.wolframite_ore.n: (Fe,Mn)WO4. Forms in quartz veins at the edge of granite. 'Tungsten' is Swedish for 'heavy stone'.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note: PbS. Forms with sphalerite in the same hydrothermal veins - look near zinc ore. Often carries silver.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note1: Just blow air through iron and it becomes steel. The colour of the flame tells you when it's done.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note: Steel = iron with only about 0.1–0.5% carbon. Pig iron (≈4% C) is hard but brittle; nearly pure wrought iron is too soft. Steel, in between, is strong and tough. Made in the Bessemer converter by blowing air through molten pig iron, burning the carbon away: C+O2→CO2. Material for turbines, pressure vessels and lathes.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note3: Announced by Henry Bessemer (UK) in 1856. Steel had been a luxury made in small crucibles; a converter made several tonnes in about 20 minutes and the price of steel collapsed. Rails, bridges and ships turned to steel. William Kelly in the USA had noticed the same principle around the same time.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note4: Early Bessemer steel kept oxygen and sulfur and was brittle. In 1856 Robert Mushet found that adding spiegeleisen (an Fe-Mn-C alloy) at the end removed the oxygen and restored the carbon (omitted: manganese is not in the mod yet). The acid lining could not remove phosphorus, so phosphorus-rich ores were useless until Thomas and Gilchrist's basic converter of 1878 [3-08].
block.semiconductor-lab.bessemer_convert: No fuel: just blow air through iron and it becomes steel.

A vessel that blows air up through molten pig iron from tuyeres in the bottom (Bessemer, 1856). No fuel: first the silicon, then the carbon burn, and that heat alone keeps the iron molten. The flame shows the progress: 1) red sparks (silicon) → 2) long white flame (the carbon "boil") → 3) the flame drops: done. In game: one iron ingot (≈ pig iron) + blower power 20 kW × 20 s → one steel ingot.

A real converter is a pear-shaped iron vessel tilted on trunnions to pour iron in and out. The blast came from a steam blowing engine. The lining is acidic silica refractory (here: refractory silica bricks [3-12]; early converters rammed ganister, a siliceous rock with clay).

Inside, mostly 2C+O2→2CO; at the mouth the CO burns in air to CO2, making the long flame. Si+O2→SiO2 releases a lot of heat, so low-silicon pig iron does not get hot enough. The end of the blow (flame drop) was judged by eye, later with a spectroscope watching the flame's light.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note: Lead sulfide PbS, the main ore of lead. Smelt it to roast it into lead oxide (PbO), then smelt that again to get lead. Galena often contains a little silver (0.01-1%); extracting it (cupellation [1-32]) is not implemented yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note1: Burning galena in air drives the sulfur out as a choking gas and leaves a yellow powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note: PbO, made by roasting galena in air: 2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2. Smelt it again: carbon and CO from the fuel take the oxygen away, PbO + C -> Pb + CO. In a furnace the SO2 escapes; roast in a reverberatory furnace [3-06] to collect it for sulfuric acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note3: Litharge is Greek for 'silver stone': it was the yellow crust left over when silver was separated from lead. It was also used in glazes, in lead glass [7-01] and in old paints.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note4: Real roasting is done below the melting point of galena (about 600-800 C) with plenty of air, so the sulfur burns off without the ore melting. In real smelters, roasting and reduction are often joined (roast-reduction), and the SO2 is sent to an acid plant.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note1: The metal of old water pipes and printing type. It is bad for your body.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note: Pb. Soft, heavy (11.3 g/cm3) and melts at only 327 C, so people have smelted it since ancient times. It does not rust away in acid easily: used for sulfuric acid chambers [6-12], containers for hydrofluoric acid [2-10] and lead-acid batteries [4-07]. Lead is toxic: it builds up in the body and harms the brain and nerves.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note3: The Romans made water pipes from lead: the Latin word plumbum gave us 'plumbing' and the symbol Pb. Gutenberg's printing type (about 1450) was a lead-tin-antimony alloy. Leaded petrol and lead paint were banned in the 20th century because of lead poisoning.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note4: Galena often contains silver. Lead was smelted first, then silver was separated by cupellation: melt the lead in air so it becomes PbO and soaks into a bone-ash dish, leaving only silver [1-32]. Much of the silver of the ancient world (and of Iwami in Japan) was made this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_trioxide: A bright yellow powder. Tungsten is hiding inside it, bound to oxygen.

WO3, made by roasting tungstic acid (H2WO4 -> WO3 + H2O). Reduce it with hydrogen in the hydrogen furnace: WO3 + 3H2 -> W + 3H2O (about 700-1000 C). Carbon is not used, because tungsten would turn into tungsten carbide.

Tungsten was first isolated in 1783 by the Elhuyar brothers in Spain, from wolframite. The name wolfram (symbol W) comes from German miners: the ore 'ate' tin like a wolf when it was mixed in tin smelting.

Industrially the reduction goes step by step through blue and violet oxides (WO2.9, WO2.72, WO2) to W. The grain size of the powder is controlled by temperature, hydrogen flow and moisture: wet hydrogen gives coarse grains, dry hydrogen fine ones. Modern plants go through ammonium paratungstate (APT).
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_powder.n: Tungsten melts at about 3400 C. Nothing can melt it, so the powder is baked together.

Metal tungsten as a grey powder. No crucible survives 3400 C, so tungsten is made by powder metallurgy: press the powder into a bar and sinter it in hydrogen (hydrogen furnace: 2 powder + 1 H2 -> sintered bar).
Powder metallurgy is how the metals that are hardest to melt are made: tungsten, molybdenum [1-31], and tungsten-carbide cutting tools.

During sintering, atoms move across the contact points between grains (diffusion), so the gaps close and the bar shrinks by about 15% while becoming dense. The temperature must be close to the melting point for this to be fast.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_bar.note: A big electric current flowing through the bar itself heats it to about 3000 C.

Pressed tungsten powder sintered in hydrogen by passing a current straight through the bar (Coolidge's method). At this stage it is still brittle like glass. Hot swaging and wire drawing make it ductile. Craft it into tungsten wire.
Before Coolidge, tungsten filaments (Just and Hanaman, 1904) were squirted paste that broke easily. Coolidge found that working the hot metal again and again made it bendable at room temperature.

Swaging: the hot bar (about 1200-1500 C) is hammered thousands of times per minute by rotating dies, little by little thinner. The grains become long fibres, which is why worked tungsten is ductile but recrystallised tungsten (after overheating) becomes brittle again.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.not: The thin wire that glows inside light bulbs and vacuum tubes.

Ductile tungsten wire (Coolidge, GE, 1909-1910). It does not melt even when glowing white-hot, so it is used for light-bulb filaments [B-01], vacuum-tube cathodes [5-02], X-ray tubes [B-03] and the needles of point-contact diodes [9-05].
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.pla: Approximation: swaging and drawing through diamond / tungsten-carbide dies are skipped (the bar becomes wire in the crafting grid).
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.not: In 1910-1911 GE began selling lamps with drawn tungsten filaments. They gave about three times more light per watt than carbon filaments, and the tungsten bulb became the light of the 20th century.

Even tungsten slowly evaporates when it glows, darkening the glass and thinning the wire. Filling the bulb with argon (Langmuir 1913, from air separation [6-07]) slowed this down; halogen lamps go further by carrying evaporated tungsten back to the filament.
block.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_furnace: Tungsten is made by blowing hydrogen over hot yellow powder.

An electric furnace [4-12] with a steel tube carrying hydrogen. (1) Reduce: WO3 + 3 H2 + 3 kW x 30 s -> W powder. (2) Sinter: 2 W powder + 1 H2 + 10 kW x 20 s -> bar. (3) GeO2 + 2 H2 + 3 kW x 20 s -> germanium (high-purity GeO2 gives GeCl4-route Ge, refinable to 10N). Hydrogen from the bag slot or an adjacent hydrogen gas holder.

Hydrogen protects the hot metal from oxygen and takes the oxygen out of the oxide. The water vapour made by the reaction leaves with the gas stream; the exhaust hydrogen is burned at the furnace exit.

Hydrogen + air is explosive (4-75%), so real furnaces purge the air with nitrogen before letting hydrogen in, and keep a small flame burning at the exit. The same furnaces later reduced GeO2 for germanium and annealed metals.
gui.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_furnace.n: Insert WO3, W powder or GeO2
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnabar_dust.not: Red powder of mercury and sulfur. Roast it to get mercury.
Crushed cinnabar HgS (from a vanilla cinnabar block, 1 -> 2). Roast it: HgS + O2 -> Hg + SO2 at about 600 C. A furnace lets the SO2 escape; a reverberatory furnace collects it.
Cinnabar was also the red pigment vermilion. The Almaden mine in Spain was worked for over 2000 years and once produced a third of the world's mercury.

Roasting works because mercury boils at 357 C: it leaves the hot ore as vapour and condenses as liquid in the cool part of the retort. The sulfur leaves as SO2, which could become sulfuric acid [2-01].
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note1: The stuff inside old thermometers. Never touch it.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note: Hg, the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Made by roasting a retort charge (cinnabar dust with an empty iron flask) in a furnace. Used for the mercury vacuum gauge; later for Sprengel and diffusion pumps and mercury lamps.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note3: Mercury is 13.6 times heavier than water, so a column only 76 cm tall balances the whole atmosphere. A water barometer would need about 10 m.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note4: Mercury vapour is toxic and builds up in the body (Minamata disease was methylmercury). It was traded in iron flasks of 34.5 kg. Gallium [1-44] melts in your hand (30 C) but is solid at room temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.placehold: Omitted: the retort's condenser (the flask just catches it). In a furnace the SO2 escapes (a reverberatory furnace collects it). Warning only: real mercury vapour is poisonous.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite_soda_c: Tungsten ore mixed with soda, ready to be melted.
Wolframite + sodium carbonate (1:1). Smelt it: (Fe,Mn)WO4 + Na2CO3 -> Na2WO4 + (Fe,Mn)O + CO2 (soda fusion, about 800-900 C).
Fusing with soda turns the insoluble ore into sodium tungstate, which dissolves in water, while iron and manganese stay behind as insoluble oxides. This is how tungsten is separated from them.
The Elhuyar brothers (1783) treated wolframite with potassium carbonate in the same way. Modern plants digest the ore with NaOH under pressure instead of fusing it.
Tungsten that now dissolves in water.
Na2WO4, the water-soluble product of soda fusion. Add hydrochloric acid to precipitate tungstic acid: Na2WO4 + 2HCl -> H2WO4 + 2NaCl.
Iron and manganese oxides do not dissolve, so leaching the fused cake with hot water and filtering leaves almost pure sodium tungstate in solution.
Sodium tungstate solutions are very dense; related tungstate salts (sodium polytungstate) are used as 'heavy liquids' to separate minerals by density.
Simplified: leaching the cake with water and filtering off the Fe/Mn oxides is skipped (they just disappear). CO2 is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungstic_acid.not: A yellow powder that falls out when acid is added.
H2WO4 (WO3*H2O), precipitated from sodium tungstate with hydrochloric acid (1 bottle = 2 mol HCl, exactly the amount needed). Roast it in a furnace to get WO3.
Scheele obtained tungstic acid from the mineral now called scheelite in 1781, but could not reduce it to the metal; the Elhuyar brothers did that two years later with charcoal.
The salt left in the liquid (NaCl) washes away. Heating H2WO4 drives off water at a few hundred degrees and leaves yellow WO3.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_germanium_t: Germanium dissolved in hydrochloric acid turns into a liquid. It still has other things mixed in.
GeO2 + 4HCl -> GeCl4 + 2H2O (2 bottles of hydrochloric acid = 4 mol HCl). Still mixed with other chlorides (AsCl3 etc.). Distil it with a quartz still.
GeCl4 is a colourless liquid that boils at only about 86 C. Most impurity chlorides boil at different temperatures, so distillation separates them.
Arsenic is the troublesome one: AsCl3 boils at 130 C, close enough that real plants add chlorine or oxidisers to keep arsenic as non-volatile As(V) during distillation.
Simplified: the impurity chlorides are only named; distilling removes them all at once.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_still.note: A quartz flask and a glass cooling tube. Boil a liquid and catch the vapour.
Use it in the crafting grid with crude GeCl4 to get distilled GeCl4. The still comes back (it is a tool, not an ingredient).
Quartz glass is used because hot HCl and chlorides do not attack it and it releases almost no impurities - ordinary glass would leach sodium and boron into the product.

The water-cooled 'Liebig condenser' was popularised by Justus von Liebig in the 1830s, although similar designs are older. Semiconductor-grade GeCl4 and SiCl4 are still purified by fractional distillation in quartz or PTFE columns.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_still.plac: Simplified: the heat source and cooling water are skipped (distillation is done in the crafting grid).
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_tetrach: Very pure germanium liquid made by boiling and cooling.
Distilled GeCl4 (bp about 86 C). Add water to hydrolyse it: GeCl4 + 2H2O -> GeO2 + 4HCl, giving high-purity GeO2.
In the 1940s-50s, Eagle-Picher and Bell Labs made transistor germanium this way: GeCl4 distillation, hydrolysis, hydrogen reduction, then zone refining.
Today GeCl4 is also the raw material for optical fibre: it is burned with SiCl4 to put GeO2 into the fibre core, raising its refractive index.
item.semiconductor-lab.high_purity_germa: Very clean white powder. Germanium from this can be refined all the way to 10N.

GeO2 from hydrolysed GeCl4. Reduce it with hydrogen in the hydrogen furnace (GeO2 + 2H2 -> Ge + 2H2O): the germanium keeps the 'GeCl4 route' mark and can reach 10N in the zone refining furnace (sulfate-route germanium stops at 9N).
It is reduced with hydrogen, not charcoal, because carbon and its ash would put impurities back in.
Zone refining removes impurities whose segregation coefficient is far from 1. Those close to 1 (and silicon in germanium) must be removed chemically first - that is why the chloride route matters.
Simplified: the HCl released by hydrolysis is not recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnetite.note1: A black stone that pulls on iron. It is full of iron.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnetite.note2: Drops from magnetite ore or iron sand (mined without Silk Touch). Four of them make a natural magnet, used to build a dynamo.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnetite.note3: Fe3O4 = FeO·Fe2O3. It mixes Fe2+ and Fe3+ ions and is the most strongly magnetic (ferrimagnetic) natural mineral. At about 72% iron by weight it is the richest iron ore, and above about 580 °C (its Curie temperature) it stops being magnetic.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnetite.note4: The word "magnet" comes from Magnesia in Greece, either because lodestones were found there or from the legend of the shepherd Magnes, whose iron-nailed sandals stuck to a rock.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite.note1: A heavy black stone. It holds the metal used for light bulb filaments.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite.note2: Mix with sodium carbonate and fire in a furnace (soda fusion) → sodium tungstate → hydrochloric acid → tungstic acid → furnace → tungsten trioxide → hydrogen furnace → tungsten powder → tungsten wire, the filament of the vacuum tube.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite.note3: (Fe,Mn)WO4 + Na2CO3 → Na2WO4 + (Fe,Mn)O + CO2. Na2WO4 dissolves in water, separating it from iron and manganese. Hydrochloric acid precipitates H2WO4, which is fired to WO3 and reduced with hydrogen: WO3 + 3H2 → W + 3H2O.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite.note4: German miners called it "wolf's froth" (Wolf Rahm) because it ate up tin when mixed into the smelt. That is where the symbol W comes from. In 1783 the Elhuyar brothers in Spain first isolated tungsten metal from this mineral.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note1: A heavy silvery stone that breaks into little cubes.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note3: Roasting (heating in air without melting): 2PbS + 3O2 → 2PbO + 2SO2. Reduction: PbO + C → Pb + CO. In the reverberatory furnace the SO2 is collected and can become sulfuric acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note4: PbS is a semiconductor (a material that conducts only a little). In 1874 Braun found that metal sulfide crystals let current flow in only one direction. Early 20th-century crystal radios touched galena with a fine wire (a cat's whisker) to turn radio waves into sound: a distant ancestor of the transistor.
block.semiconductor-lab.magnetite_ore.no: Iron ore deep underground that can become a magnet.

Banded iron formations formed about 2.5 to 1.8 billion years ago. Oxygen released by cyanobacteria (photosynthetic bacteria) oxidized iron (Fe²⁺) dissolved in the sea and made it settle out, laying down stripes of iron oxide and quartz.

Tiny magnetite crystals exist in living things too: magnetotactic bacteria line up magnetite grains inside themselves as a compass needle. Near huge magnetite deposits such as Kiruna in Sweden, compasses go wrong.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note1: Black beach sand. It sticks to a magnet.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note3: In tatara ironmaking, iron sand and charcoal are fed in turns and reduced by carbon monoxide: Fe3O4 + 4CO → 3Fe + 4CO2. The iron does not fully melt; a lump called kera forms at the bottom, and its best part becomes tamahagane steel.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note4: One tatara run (three days and nights, called hitoyo) uses about 10 t of iron sand and 12 t of charcoal to make about 2.5 t of kera. The Nittoho tatara in Shimane still runs each winter to supply steel for Japanese swords.
block.semiconductor-lab.wolframite_ore.n: Ore holding tungsten, a very heavy metal.

As granite magma cools, the last hot water (hydrothermal fluid) carries dissolved tungsten and tin into cracks, where they crystallize in quartz veins as it cools. That is why wolframite is often found with tin ore (cassiterite).
Tungsten melts at 3422 °C, the highest of any metal, and its density (about 19.3 g/cm³) is almost the same as gold. Today China produces about 80% of the world's tungsten.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note1: Lead ore. Look for it near zinc ore.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note3: Lead and zinc dissolved in hot underground brines (hydrothermal fluids) precipitate as sulfides when they meet sulfur-bearing water: Pb²⁺ + H2S → PbS + 2H⁺. That is why galena (PbS) and sphalerite (ZnS) form together.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note4: Its crystals have the same cubic structure as table salt, so it cleaves into neat little cubes. Ancient Egyptians ground galena into kohl, the dark eyeliner painted around the eyes.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_ash.note1: What is left after burning coal. It holds a tiny bit of germanium.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_ash.note2: Smelt coal in a furnace. 8 of them make germanium concentrate.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_ash.note3: Germanium binds to the plant matter that became coal, so some coals hold a few hundred ppm. Burning sends the carbon off as CO2 while the Ge stays concentrated in the ash, especially the fine fly ash.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_ash.note4: In 1930 the Norwegian geochemist V. M. Goldschmidt reported that rare elements such as germanium are strongly enriched in coal ash. Coal from places like Lincang in Yunnan, China is still a major germanium source.
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_concent: A powder with the germanium gathered and concentrated.
From 8 coal ash, or as a by-product of roasting sphalerite in the reverberatory furnace. Combine with sulfuric acid to get germanium dioxide.
Real concentrate is a mix of oxides and sulfides with a few percent germanium (for example zinc-smelting residue). Acid dissolves it so the germanium can be separated from the other metals.

Germanium was discovered in 1886 by Clemens Winkler in the silver ore argyrodite (Ag8GeS6). It matched Mendeleev's 1871 prediction of 'eka-silicon' (atomic weight about 72, density about 5.5) and became proof that the periodic table worked.
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_dioxide: A white powder of germanium joined to oxygen.
Made from germanium concentrate + sulfuric acid (crude, up to 9N) or by breaking down GeCl4 with water (high purity, up to 10N). Reduce it with charcoal or in the hydrogen furnace to get germanium.

GeO2 is a sibling of SiO2 (quartz) and can take the same crystal form. Hydrogen reduces it: GeO2 + 2H2 -> Ge + 2H2O (about 600-700 °C). Charcoal also works (GeO2 + C -> Ge + CO2) but leaves a little carbon behind.
GeO2 is mixed into the core of optical fibres: it raises the refractive index so light stays trapped in the core. Pure GeO2 glass passes infrared well and is used in infrared optics.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note1: Black, slippery carbon - the same stuff as pencil lead.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note3: Sheets of hexagonal carbon nets stacked in layers. The layers are held only by weak van der Waals forces, so they slide off onto paper. It does not melt at normal pressure: it sublimes (solid straight to gas) at about 3600 °C.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note4: In the 1560s a large vein of pure graphite was found at Borrowdale in England, and the pencil was born. People thought it was a kind of lead and called it 'plumbago'. In 1789 Abraham Werner named it graphite, from the Greek graphein, 'to write'.
block.semiconductor-lab.graphite_ore.not: Mine it for graphite, used for electrolyzer electrodes and boats.
Natural graphite is carbon from ancient living things rearranged into graphite by heat and pressure (metamorphism). It comes as flake, lump (vein) and amorphous graphite.
Sri Lankan vein graphite is a rare lump graphite over 90% pure. It is thought to have been deposited from hot underground fluids.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium.note1: A soft silver metal you can scratch with a fingernail.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium.note2: A by-product of roasting sphalerite in the reverberatory furnace. As a dopant in the refiner it makes p-type germanium; sandwich n-type Ge with it and fire to make an alloy-junction transistor.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium.note3: Indium is in group 13 (the boron family) with 3 outer electrons. Inside 4-electron germanium it leaves one bond short - a 'hole' - which makes p-type material. Its low melting point (about 157 °C) makes it easy to melt onto Ge as an alloy.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium.note4: Discovered in 1863 by Reich and Richter in sphalerite; its indigo spectral line gave it the name. Bend it and it 'cries' like tin. Today it is essential for the transparent electrodes (ITO, indium tin oxide) in phone screens.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_germanium.not: Made by reducing germanium dioxide with charcoal or in the hydrogen furnace. Refine it in the zone refining furnace: 6N -> 9N -> 10N.
At this stage the purity is about 99-99.9% (2N-3N). A transistor needs 9N (99.9999999%) or better: at most one impurity atom per billion.

Germanium looks like a metal but is a semiconductor, with the same crystal structure as diamond - hard and brittle. It melts at about 938 °C and, like water, expands when it freezes (the solid floats on the liquid).
item.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite.note1: An ore of zinc and sulfur, with a few rare metals mixed in.
item.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite.note2: Drops from sphalerite ore. A furnace gives zinc; roasting in the reverberatory furnace gives zinc oxide + SO2, with germanium concentrate or indium as by-products.
item.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite.note3: ZnS. Roasting: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. Elements similar to zinc - germanium, indium, cadmium, gallium - hide in its crystal and collect in the residue after the zinc is taken out.
item.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite.note4: The name comes from the Greek sphaleros, 'deceptive': it looks like lead ore (galena) but yields no lead. Its German name, blende, also means 'the deceiver'.
block.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite_ore.n: Mine it for sphalerite. Found at the same depths as galena.
Sphalerite and galena usually precipitate together from hot underground water (lead-zinc deposits). Iron-rich sphalerite is black; iron-poor crystals are clear yellow or red.
The zinc-blende crystal structure is shared by many compound semiconductors such as gallium arsenide (GaAs). It is the diamond structure of Ge and Si with its two sites filled by different elements.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_ingot.note1: A bar of zinc, used for galvanized iron and batteries.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_ingot.note2: Smelt sphalerite in a furnace, or roast it to zinc oxide in the reverberatory furnace and then reduce that in a furnace.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_ingot.note3: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. The roughly 1000 °C needed is above zinc's boiling point (about 907 °C), so the zinc comes off as vapour. It burns back to oxide in air, so it has to be condensed away from air.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_ingot.note4: Zinc distillation began at Zawar in India (worked from around the 12th century to the early 19th); in Europe William Champion patented it in 1738. Galvanized iron is iron plated with zinc: the zinc corrodes first and protects the iron (sacrificial protection).
block.semiconductor-lab.borax_deposit.no: A layer of white crystals at the bottom of a dried-up desert lake.
Found near the surface of deserts (y56-76) in sand and sandstone, a little rarer than trona. A wooden pickaxe gives borax; silk touch gives the block.

In dry regions boron leached from volcanic rocks drains into lakes; when the water evaporates it crystallizes as an evaporite. At Searles Lake in California trona and borax come out of the same lake bed.
In the 1880s borax from Death Valley was hauled about 260 km to the railway in huge wagons pulled by twenty mules (the '20 Mule Team'). Today Turkey holds most of the world's boron reserves.
item.semiconductor-lab.borax.note1: A white mineral with boron in it. It is also used to make slime.
item.semiconductor-lab.borax.note2: Mined from borax deposits. With sulfuric acid it gives 2 boric acid (1 item = 2 mol).
item.semiconductor-lab.borax.note3: Na2B4O7·10H2O (sodium tetraborate decahydrate). Sulfuric acid, the stronger acid, drives out the weak boric acid: Na2B4O7·10H2O + H2SO4 -> 4H3BO3 + Na2SO4 + 5H2O.
item.semiconductor-lab.borax.note4: In the Middle Ages borax (tincal) from Tibetan lakes travelled the Silk Road. Molten borax dissolves the oxide film on metals, so it has long been the flux for brazing gold and silver.
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.note1: A very weak acid, once used in eye wash and in cockroach bait.
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.note2: Borax + sulfuric acid gives 2. 1 item = 2 mol. Bake it in a furnace to get boron trioxide (the water comes off).
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.note3: H3BO3 = B(OH)3. Instead of giving off H+ like an ordinary acid, it takes OH- from water and becomes B(OH)4- (a Lewis acid, pKa about 9.2). Heating drives off water: 2H3BO3 -> B2O3 + 3H2O (in the game 1 item = 2 mol, so 1 -> 1).
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.note4: In Tuscany, Italy, steam jets from the ground carry boric acid; from 1818 it was boiled down there (Larderello). The same steam ran the world's first geothermal power generator in 1904.
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.placeh: Omitted: the sodium sulfate (Na2SO4) and water formed along with it are discarded.
item.semiconductor-lab.boron_trioxide.no: A glassy lump of boron and oxygen - the stuff that makes silicon p-type.

Bake boric acid in a furnace. 1 item = 1 mol. A p-type dopant for silicon (used in the v0.2b silicon chapter), and an ingredient of heat-resistant borosilicate glass [2-15]. In silicon, put it in the CZ puller [9-08] dopant slot (p-type).

B2O3 melts into a glass at about 450 °C. Boron is in group 13 with 3 electrons; inside silicon (group 14, 4 electrons) it leaves one bond short - a hole - making p-type. Its segregation coefficient in silicon is about 0.8, close to 1, so the concentration barely changes along a pulled crystal - which is why boron is the p-type dopant of choice for silicon.

Elemental boron was isolated almost simultaneously in 1808 by Gay-Lussac and Thénard and by Davy, but pure boron was not made until Weintraub in 1909. In the 1950s Bell Labs diffused boron into silicon surfaces with heat to make p-type layers (the diffusion process) - a foundation of how integrated circuits are made.
block.semiconductor-lab.quartz_vein.note: A crack in the rock filled with white quartz.
Common everywhere in stone and deepslate (y-56 to 96). Mine with a stone pickaxe or better for vein quartz; silk touch gives the block.

Hot water deep underground (hydrothermal fluid) dissolves SiO2 from the rock and deposits it as quartz in cracks when it cools or the pressure drops. About 12% of the Earth's crust is quartz, the most common mineral after feldspar. Quartz veins sometimes carry gold (gold-quartz veins).
Where a vein has open space, quartz grows into clear hexagonal crystals - rock crystal. In Kofu, Yamanashi, crystal has been mined since the Edo period, and crystal carving became a local industry.
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.note1: A white stone of almost pure silicon dioxide (SiO2) - the starting point for glass and silicon.
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.note2: Mined from quartz veins. Melt it in the oxyhydrogen burner to get fused quartz. Also the raw material for metallurgical silicon [1-15] later on.
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.note3: SiO2 is a crystal of tetrahedra - one silicon surrounded by four oxygens - linked by sharing their corner oxygens. It melts at about 1713 °C, far beyond a furnace (about 1000 °C). Fused quartz is made from quartz low in iron, aluminium and other impurities (natural rock crystal or selected vein quartz).
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.note4: The purest natural quartz today comes from pegmatites (very coarse granite) at Spruce Pine, North Carolina, with under 100 ppm impurities. It becomes the quartz crucibles that silicon single crystals are pulled from - holding up the world's semiconductor industry.
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.place: Omitted: real quartz is crushed and acid-washed to remove iron and other impurities before melting (the purification steps).
item.semiconductor-lab.metallurgical_sil: Shiny grey silicon made from stone, charcoal and a lot of electricity.

From the arc furnace: 2 vein quartz + 1 charcoal or coal. 98% pure (metallurgical grade) - still far too dirty for semiconductors, so it is purified via trichlorosilane [1-16] and the Siemens process [1-17]. Each kg takes over 10 kWh of electricity. Modern plants use AC submerged-arc furnaces; the game approximates it with DC until AC arrives in v0.4.

SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO. Silicon and oxygen are bound so tightly that ordinary furnace temperatures cannot separate them; the arc's ~2000 °C is needed. Remaining impurities are iron, aluminium, calcium and so on (from the raw materials and electrodes).

Most metallurgical silicon goes into aluminium alloys and silicone resins, not semiconductors. Because it uses so much electricity, plants have been built where hydropower is cheap, such as Norway. The fine SiO2 dust from the furnace (silica fume) is used to make high-strength concrete.
Omitted: carbon monoxide (CO) and SiO fumes are not collected. Industrial production in electric furnaces began in the early 20th century (c. 1900; no exact year is known).
block.semiconductor-lab.trichlorosilane_: Turns hard silicon into a liquid, then boils it again and again to clean it.

Synthesis (10 kW, 60 s): metallurgical silicon 1 + dry hydrogen chloride 3 → crude trichlorosilane 1 (99%) + hydrogen 1. Distillation (20 kW, 30 s per stage): put trichlorosilane in the bottom-left slot; each stage removes 9/10 of the impurities (one more 9), up to 11N. If the distillation slot has something, it distils; otherwise it synthesizes. Use dry HCl gas from the HCl burner with no water, not hydrochloric acid.

Si + 3HCl → SiHCl3 + H2 at about 300 °C (the reaction gives off heat). SiHCl3 boils at 32 °C, BCl3 at 12 °C and PCl3 at 76 °C, so a distillation column can separate the boron and phosphorus chlorides by their boiling points.

Boron and phosphorus are the hardest impurities, because they are the very elements that set a semiconductor's type. Real plants use tall columns with many trays and repeat the distillation. It is the same idea as distilling GeCl4 for germanium.

Approximation: real plants use a fluidized-bed reactor plus separate tall distillation columns; here it is one block. ⚠️ Amounts are symbolic (1 silicon ≈ 1 kg but 1 gas bag = 1 mol). ⚠️ Power and time are for gameplay. By-product SiCl4 and waste chlorides are not shown.
gui.semiconductor-lab.trichlorosilane_re: Needs Si 1 + HCl gas 3, or TCS to distil
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_chloride: The sharp-smelling gas that becomes hydrochloric acid when it dissolves in water. Here it is kept dry.
From the HCl burner with no water: H2 1 mol + Cl2 1 mol → hydrogen chloride 2 bags (1 bag = 1 mol). Used for trichlorosilane [1-16]. The Siemens reactor [1-17] gives it back.
HCl is a colourless gas that dissolves very easily in water (that is hydrochloric acid). Trichlorosilane reacts with water, so silicon refining needs dry HCl gas, not the acid.

Wet HCl eats through steel, but dry HCl hardly does, so keeping the gas dry protects the plant too. In real plants the HCl from the Siemens reactor is separated and sent back to make more trichlorosilane.
Approximation: real HCl is stored in cylinders or piped; here it is a 1 mol bag.
item.semiconductor-lab.trichlorosilane.n: Silicon turned into a liquid. It boils at a bath-like temperature, so it is easy to clean by distilling.
SiHCl3. From the trichlorosilane reactor: crude is 99%. Put it back in the distillation slot: each stage adds one 9 (up to 11N). Feed it to the Siemens reactor [1-17] to make polysilicon.
A colourless liquid that boils at 32 °C. It fumes in moist air (it reacts with water and gives off HCl), so it is handled sealed and dry.
Solid silicon cannot be distilled, but its chloride can. The trick of 'make it a liquid, distil it, turn it back' is the key to ultra-pure silicon, just like GeCl4 for germanium.
item.semiconductor-lab.trichlorosilane.p: Approximation: 1 item is a symbolic amount (enough for about 1 kg of silicon). ⚠️ Crude purity 99% is a game stage.
Thin silicon rods glow hot inside a bell, and grow fatter and fatter from the gas.

500 kW (one steam turbine). Trichlorosilane distilled to 9N or more 1 + hydrogen 1 → polysilicon 1 (same purity, 9N–11N) + hydrogen chloride gas 3 (648 s = 90 kWh). The HCl goes back to the trichlorosilane reactor [1-16]. Not enough power → stops (the rods cannot stay at 1100 °C).

SiHCl3 + H2 → Si + 3HCl at about 1100 °C. Electricity flows through the silicon rods themselves to heat them, so the walls stay cooler and add little dirt. Only silicon sticks to the rods, layer by layer.

11N means one foreign atom in a hundred billion, like one stranger among more than ten times the people on Earth. A rod grows about 1 mm per hour and takes days to reach 15–20 cm thick. Siemens developed the method in the mid-1950s (basic patent filed 1956, published 1959).

Omitted: the thin seed rods (slim rods) and pre-heating them (cold silicon barely conducts). ⚠️ Amounts are symbolic (1 polysilicon ≈ 1 kg but 1 gas bag = 1 mol). 90 kWh/kg is a patent comparative example; modern reactors use less ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.note1: The cleanest stuff people make in large amounts: silicon with almost nothing else in it.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.note2: From the Siemens reactor [1-17]: same purity as the trichlorosilane (9N–11N). Made of many tiny crystals. Next it becomes one big crystal (CZ [9-08], FZ [9-09]) and then wafers.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.note3: "Poly" means many crystals: the silicon that piles up on the rod grows as countless small grains facing different ways. For transistors it must be melted and regrown as a single crystal.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.note4: Most polysilicon goes to solar cells (lower purity is enough); the purest goes to chips. Every year the world makes over a million tonnes ⚠️, mostly by the Siemens method.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.place: Approximation: 1 item ≈ 1 kg (symbolic amounts, Q22-1). Real rods are crushed into chunks for the crucible.
block.semiconductor-lab.malachite_ore.no: Rock with green banded stone in it, the same green as rusted copper.
In stone near the surface (y40-110). A stone pickaxe or better drops malachite. It forms in the 'oxidized zone' at the top of a copper deposit, exposed to rain and air.

Deep copper ore (chalcopyrite, the vanilla copper ore) turns into green malachite and blue azurite near the surface where it meets water and carbon dioxide. People once looked for copper by this eye-catching green.

Below the oxidized zone lies an 'enriched zone' where dissolved copper settled, and below that the original sulfide ore. When ancient mines exhausted the surface malachite they hit sulfide ore, which is harder to smelt [1-04].
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.note1: A green stone. Bake it with charcoal and copper comes out.
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.note2: Basic copper carbonate Cu2CO3(OH)2. Furnace (faster in a blast furnace) -> copper ingot. Heat splits it into CuO, CO2 and H2O, and carbon (CO) from the fuel takes the oxygen: CuO + C -> Cu + CO.
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.note3: At Belovode in Serbia, slag from copper smelting about 7000 years ago (around 5000 BC) has been found. The smelters used a manganese-rich, greenish-black oxidized copper ore, and kept pure malachite for beads. In ancient Egypt malachite was also ground and worn as eye paint.
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.note4: Malachite decomposes into black copper oxide at about 300 C, and carbon monoxide in a charcoal fire reduces it from about 800 C. Copper melts at 1085 C, so a furnace blown with bellows was needed to melt it into a lump. Having no sulfur, it is easier than sulfide ore and became the first copper ore used.
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.placeho: Approximation: the furnace (~1000 C) does reduction and melting in one step (reduced by the fuel's C/CO, as in CHEMISTRY #38). CO2 and steam are not collected.
Granite with dark, heavy grains in it. Tin ore.
Only in granite (y-10-70, the same belt as wolframite). An iron pickaxe or better drops cassiterite.
Tin and tungsten often settle together in the same veins from the last hot water left as granite cools. Cornwall in England has produced tin since the Bronze Age.

Cassiterite is very heavy (density about 7) and does not weather. When rock breaks down it stays behind and gathers in river sand (placer deposits). Big tin mines in Malaysia and Indonesia dig such river and sea sands (in the game it is only in granite).
item.semiconductor-lab.cassiterite.note1: A dark, heavy stone. Bake it with charcoal and tin comes out.
item.semiconductor-lab.cassiterite.note2: Tin(IV) oxide SnO2. Hard (Mohs 6-7). Bake it in a furnace with charcoal (the fuel's carbon) for a tin ingot [1-30].
item.semiconductor-lab.cassiterite.note3: The name comes from the Greek for tin (kassiteros). To make bronze with copper, ancient people carried tin long distances and traded it.
item.semiconductor-lab.cassiterite.note4: SnO2 hardly dissolves in water or acids; it is a very stable oxide, so it survives weathering at the surface. Thin transparent SnO2 films conduct electricity, and are used today for insulating window coatings and solar cell electrodes (FTO).
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.note1: A soft, silvery metal. Mixed with copper it makes bronze.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.note2: Cassiterite -> furnace (faster in a blast furnace). SnO2 + 2C -> Sn + 2CO (reduced by the fuel's carbon). Melts at only 232 C. A material for bronze [1-05] and speculum metal [7-05].
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.note3: Bend a tin bar and it creaks (the 'tin cry'): crystals rubbing against each other. Left in the cold for a long time it crumbles into grey powder (tin pest, a change that happens below 13 C).
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.note4: Tin, a bronze material 5000 years ago, is now the main part of electronic solder and even the light source of cutting-edge EUV lithography [7-18]: droplets of molten tin about 30 um across are hit by a laser tens of thousands of times a second, becoming a plasma that emits 13.5 nm light.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.placeho: Approximation: the furnace (~1000 C) does reduction and melting in one step (reduced by the fuel's C/CO, as in CHEMISTRY #38). CO and CO2 are not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.bronze_charge.not: Copper and tin weighed and mixed. Melt it and it becomes bronze.
8 copper ingots + 1 tin ingot -> 9 (about 11% tin). Melt in a furnace (faster in a blast furnace) for bronze ingots.
Ancient founders varied the copper-tin ratio: about one tenth tin for tools and swords, over one fifth for bells (hard, ringing bell metal).
Tin dissolves readily in molten copper. The alloy melts lower (copper 1085 C -> bronze about 950 C) and flows into every corner of a mould, so it casts well.
item.semiconductor-lab.bronze_ingot.note: Copper with one tenth tin: a metal that melts easily yet is hard.
Cu-Sn about 11%. Much harder than pure copper and corrodes less. c:ingots/bronze. With more tin, speculum metal makes mirrors [7-05].

From about 3000 BC people made tools, weapons, mirrors and bells of bronze (the Bronze Age). Before that, copper containing arsenic (arsenical bronze) was also used (⚠️ timing and spread differ by region).
Large tin atoms in the copper crystal distort the lattice and hinder the slipping of crystal planes (solid-solution strengthening), so the alloy is harder than the pure metal.
item.semiconductor-lab.bronze_ingot.plac: Approximation: melting in a furnace stands in for a crucible furnace (CHEMISTRY #38).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_ash.note1: White ash from burnt bone. It soaks up molten metal oxides well.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_ash.note2: Bone meal -> furnace. Mostly calcium phosphate. 4 make a cupel.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_ash.note3: Besides cupels, bone ash goes into English 'bone china' (white porcelain with bone ash in it).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_ash.note4: Burning removes the bone's organic part (collagen), leaving porous hydroxyapatite Ca5(PO4)3(OH). Molten lead oxide wets it and soaks in by capillary action, but molten silver is repelled and stays on the surface.
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel.note1: A small dish of pressed bone ash. Heat silver-bearing lead on it and only the silver remains.
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel.note2: 4 bone ash. Combine with 8 lead ingots into a cupel charge (the dish soaks up lead oxide and is used up).
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel.note3: 'Cupel' comes from the Latin for 'little cup'. The same dishes have long been used in assaying, testing the purity of gold and silver.
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel.note4: A cupel must weigh about as much as the lead oxide it absorbs. Old mines also used hearths of pressed wood ash or lime besides bone ash.
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel_charge.note: Silver-bearing lead on a cupel. Heat it in a blast furnace and silver comes out.
8 lead ingots + cupel. Blast furnace (blown with air), about 1000 C -> silver nugget. A plain furnace does not give enough air.

At Iwami Ginzan in Japan, silver was extracted by cupellation introduced from the Korean peninsula in 1533, and in the 16th-17th centuries it produced a large share of the world's silver (⚠️ the share varies by source).

Air on molten lead gives 2Pb + O2 -> 2PbO. PbO melts at 888 C and soaks into the cupel or runs off. Silver hardly oxidizes, so when all the lead is gone a bright silver bead appears (the 'flash' or 'blick').
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel_charge.plac: Approximation: all galena is treated as silver-bearing, 1 silver nugget per 8 lead (about 1.4%). Real silver content is about 0.01-1% and varies. The PbO (litharge) absorbed by the cupel is not recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.silver_nugget.not: A bead of silver left by cupellation. 9 make a silver ingot.
Cupel charge -> blast furnace. Used in vacuum evaporation [5-14] to coat glass thinly for half-mirrors and mirrors.
Much of the silver in old coins and silverware was extracted from galena by cupellation.
Silver reflects visible light better than any other metal (over 95%), but it tarnishes black with sulfur compounds (silver sulfide).
item.semiconductor-lab.silver_ingot.note: A shining white metal. It conducts electricity and heat best of all.
9 silver nuggets (an ingot can be split back into 9). c:ingots/silver.
Used for photographic emulsions (silver bromide and iodide), mirrors and electrical contacts.

Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of all metals (slightly above copper), yet copper is the main wiring metal because it is far cheaper. Chip wiring moved from aluminum to copper, and silver is hardly used.
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorite.note1: A glassy purple or green stone. It contains fluorine.
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorite.note2: Calcium fluoride CaF2. Mined from fluorite ore with a stone pickaxe or better. Raw material for hydrofluoric acid [2-10] (fluorite + sulfuric acid).
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorite.note3: The first record is 'fluores' in Agricola's 1530 book: a flux that made ores melt and flow more easily in the furnace, from Latin fluere, to flow. The element fluorine is named after it.
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorite.note4: Some fluorite glows blue under ultraviolet light; in 1852 Stokes named this glow 'fluorescence' after it. The Japanese name means 'firefly stone' because it glows when heated. Large fluorite crystals later became lenses and windows for excimer laser lithography [7-20].
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorite_ore.not: Stone with purple and green grains in it. Mining it gives fluorite.
Found in stone and deepslate at the same depth as galena (Y −16 to 64), less often than galena. Stone pickaxe or better. Silk Touch keeps the ore block.
Fluorite usually forms in veins left by hot water flowing through cracks in rock (hydrothermal veins), together with galena and sphalerite. Lead and zinc mines often produce fluorite too.
Most fluorite today becomes hydrofluoric acid, the starting point of almost all fluorine chemistry (fluoropolymers, refrigerants, etching gases for chips).
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorite_ore.pla: Approximation: real fluorite occurs in veins with galena and sphalerite; in the game it is scattered at the same depth.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_flask.note1: An iron bottle for mercury. Mercury does not dissolve iron.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_flask.note2: Roast it together with cinnabar dust and the mercury that comes out collects in this flask.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_flask.note3: Mercury mixes with gold, silver, copper and zinc to form amalgams, but hardly with iron. That is why mercury is kept in iron.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_flask.note4: Mercury is still traded by the flask: one flask is 76 pounds (about 34.5 kg), and prices are quoted per flask.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_bottle.note1: A lead bottle for hydrofluoric acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_bottle.note2: Hydrofluoric acid dissolves glass, so it cannot go in a glass bottle.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_bottle.note3: ⚠️ Hydrofluoric acid used to be kept in lead, wax (ceresin) or gutta-percha (a tree resin) containers. Today it comes in polyethylene bottles.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_bottle.note4: A thin film of lead fluoride (PbF2) forms on lead and slows further attack. Sulfuric acid forms a lead sulfate film, which is why lead lined the chambers of the lead-chamber process.
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnabar_retort_c: Cinnabar dust packed with an empty iron flask. Roast it to collect mercury.
Roast it in a furnace or a reverberatory furnace to get an iron flask of mercury (the reverberatory furnace also gives SO2).
HgS + O2 → Hg (gas) + SO2. Mercury boils at 357 °C, so it leaves as vapour; it is cooled back to liquid and caught in the flask.
At the Almadén mine in Spain, mercury vapour was cooled and collected for centuries in rows of clay pipes called aludels. The vapour is very toxic and ruined the health of the workers.
item.semiconductor-lab.coke.note1: What is left after baking coal: a light, grey, holey kind of charcoal.
item.semiconductor-lab.coke.note2: The gas works retort [2-20] turns 4 coal into 3 coke. It fuels the retort and the blast furnace [1-09] in place of charcoal (the coke blast furnace [1-10]).
item.semiconductor-lab.coke.note3: Raw coal gives off smoke and sulfur that make iron brittle. Baking off the volatile part leaves almost pure carbon, a strong fuel. In 1709 Darby made iron with coke, ending the worry of using up the forests.
item.semiconductor-lab.coke.note4: In a blast furnace, coke does three jobs: fuel, carbon that reduces the iron ore, and a frame that holds up the charge. Because it is full of holes, the air blast can pass through it.
item.semiconductor-lab.bauxite.note1: A reddish-brown, earthy rock. The raw material of aluminium.
item.semiconductor-lab.bauxite.note2: A mixture of aluminium hydroxides (gibbsite Al(OH)3 and others) and red iron rust (iron oxide). Mined from bauxite ore. Dissolved in sodium hydroxide to extract alumina (Bayer process [1-14]).
item.semiconductor-lab.bauxite.note3: Where it is hot and rainy, rock washed by rain for a very long time loses its soluble parts, leaving aluminium and iron behind (residual weathering). The red is the colour of iron rust.
item.semiconductor-lab.bauxite.note4: In 1821 Berthier found it near the village of Les Baux in southern France and named it after the village. Today tropical and subtropical countries such as Australia and Guinea are the big producers.
block.semiconductor-lab.bauxite_ore.note: A reddish-brown ore near the surface in jungles and savannas.
Only in jungles and savannas, replacing dirt, coarse dirt and stone at Y 56–90. Mine with a pickaxe (wood is fine). Silk Touch keeps the ore block.
Bauxite usually lies near the surface like a blanket rather than deep underground, so it is dug in open pits.
The 'red mud' left after extracting aluminium is strongly alkaline. As the 2010 reservoir collapse at Ajka, Hungary showed, how to store it is a serious problem.
block.semiconductor-lab.bauxite_ore.plac: Approximation: it appears as lumps in dirt and stone rather than as a real surface layer (laterite).
block.semiconductor-lab.bayer_digester.n: A vessel that dissolves bauxite in hot caustic soda and takes out only the aluminium part.

2 kW. 2 bauxite → 1 aluminium hydroxide + 1 red mud (30 s). The liquor is 1 sodium hydroxide dissolved in 1 water bucket and lasts 4 runs (the empty bucket goes to the output). Bake aluminium hydroxide in a furnace to get alumina.

Al(OH)3 + NaOH → NaAl(OH)4. The aluminium dissolves, but iron rust does not and stays behind as red mud. Cooling the filtered liquor and adding seed crystals brings aluminium hydroxide back out. The liquor is used again and again.

Karl Josef Bayer devised it in 1888 while working for textile mills in Russia. Paired with the Hall–Héroult process of two years earlier, these two methods still make almost all the world's aluminium. Gallium collects in the liquor, and most gallium today comes from here.
block.semiconductor-lab.bayer_digester.p: Omitted: heating is an electric heater (the real one is a steam-heated pressure vessel at about 150–250 °C). Amounts are symbolic (really about 2–3 tonnes of bauxite per tonne of alumina). Gallium in the liquor is not extracted.
item.semiconductor-lab.aluminium_hydroxi: A white powder. Baking it gives alumina.
Al(OH)3, from the Bayer digester [1-14]. Bake it in a furnace or blast furnace to get alumina Al2O3 (the water leaves). Also used to make cryolite [1-38].
2Al(OH)3 → Al2O3 + 3H2O. Real plants bake it at over about 1000 °C (calcination).
It is also used in antacids and as a flame retardant (it releases water when heated and cools the fire).
item.semiconductor-lab.alumina.note1: White powder of aluminium oxide. The raw material of aluminium.
item.semiconductor-lab.alumina.note2: Al2O3, made by baking aluminium hydroxide. Its melting point (about 2050 °C) is too high, so it is dissolved in molten cryolite and electrolysed (Hall–Héroult process [1-29]).
item.semiconductor-lab.alumina.note3: Alumina crystals are very hard; the gems ruby (with chromium) and sapphire (with iron and titanium) are alumina too. It is also used as an abrasive and refractory.
item.semiconductor-lab.alumina.note4: Aluminium is the most common metal in the Earth's crust, but it holds oxygen so tightly that it was very hard to extract before electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_mud.note1: The red mud left after taking out aluminium. It is strongly alkaline, so do not touch it with bare hands.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_mud.note2: Residue of the Bayer digester [1-14]: iron oxides (the red colour), silicon and titanium compounds and leftover caustic soda. No use yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_mud.note3: About 1–1.5 tonnes of red mud come out per tonne of alumina. It is dried in ponds, which take up space and must be watched so the alkali does not leak.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_mud.note4: In October 2010 a red mud reservoir burst at Ajka, Hungary, and strongly alkaline mud flowed into villages and rivers (ten people died). Since then, drying it into solid blocks and reusing it for cement and iron have been studied more.
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.note1: An icy, white, see-through mineral. It becomes the 'hot bath' for making aluminium.
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.note2: Na3AlF6. At the crafting table: 3 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles come back) + 1 aluminium hydroxide + 3 sodium hydroxide → 1 cryolite (6HF + Al(OH)3 + 3NaOH → Na3AlF6 + 6H2O). The bath for the Hall–Héroult process [1-29].
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.note3: Alumina only melts at about 2050 °C, but it dissolves well in cryolite melted at about 1000 °C, so it can be electrolysed at about 960 °C. That is the key idea of the Hall–Héroult process.
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.note4: Natural cryolite was mined in quantity only at Ivittuut, Greenland, and ran out in 1987. Today it is all made chemically (this way). ⚠️ The year synthetic production became industrial is not yet checked.
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.placehol: Approximation: mixed at the crafting table (really reacted in lead- or rubber-lined tanks, then the crystals are filtered and dried).
block.semiconductor-lab.hall_heroult_cel: A cell that dissolves alumina in molten cryolite and takes out aluminium with electricity. It eats a lot of power.

100 kW. 2 alumina → 1 aluminium (about 1 kg, 540 s = 15 kWh). 1 cryolite gives a bath for 16 runs; 1 graphite rod (anode) lasts 2 runs. 2Al2O3 + 3C → 4Al + 3CO2. The current's own heat keeps the bath at about 960 °C.

In 1886 Charles Martin Hall (22, USA) and Paul Héroult (23, France) found the same method independently. Both were born in 1863 and both died in 1914. Before that, aluminium cost more than gold or silver, and Napoleon III is said to have served only his most honoured guests on aluminium plates.

About 13–15 kWh (roughly a household's daily use) goes into 1 kg of aluminium, so smelters were built near hydropower (Niagara, Norway, Canada). Aluminium is called 'packaged electricity'; recycling it needs only about 5% of the energy of making it new.

Omitted: CO2 and fluoride exhaust are not modelled, nor current and voltage (really about 4–5 V DC at tens to hundreds of thousands of amperes). One block stands for a whole potline of dozens of cells.
item.semiconductor-lab.aluminium_ingot.n: A light, silvery metal that hardly rusts.
Made in the Hall–Héroult cell [1-29]. Later used for chip wiring (vacuum evaporation [9-25]) and machine parts.
In air, aluminium quickly grows a thin oxide film (alumina) that protects the metal underneath, so rust does not spread, the same trick silicon uses with its oxide.
In 1959 Noyce's integrated circuit was wired with aluminium evaporated onto the chip. IC wiring stayed aluminium until copper took over in the 1990s.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_tetrachlo: A liquid made alongside trichlorosilane. It fumes white in air. ⚠ Reacts with water, releasing hydrochloric acid gas.
SiCl4. One per 4 syntheses in the trichlorosilane reactor (Si + 4HCl -> SiCl4 + 2H2). Burned in the oxyhydrogen burner into synthetic quartz; later a material for epitaxy [9-30]. Boils at 57.6 C.

Polysilicon plants produce several times more SiCl4 than trichlorosilane as a byproduct. Rather than dump it, they turn it into synthetic quartz and optical-fibre feedstock, or convert it back to trichlorosilane with hydrogen.
SiCl4 reacts with moisture in air to give fine SiO2 particles and HCl (the white fumes). Done inside a flame, this reaction yields an extremely pure glass powder that is fused into synthetic quartz.
Approximation: one per 4 syntheses is a game value (in reality 10-20% of the product). No bottle.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_grain.no: Tiny grains of platinum mixed into river and beach sand. Very rare.
Native platinum (Pt with palladium, iridium, iron and others). Digging beach iron sand with a shovel rarely (about 3%) gives some (not with Silk Touch). Refined by dissolving in aqua regia [1-18].

Platinum is heavy and never rusts, so when rock breaks down it stays metal and settles with iron sand and gold in riverbeds and beaches (placer deposits). It came from rivers in Colombia and the Urals.
Gold miners in Colombia threw away the hard-to-melt white grains as 'platina' (little silver). In 1748 Ulloa's travel account first described it in Europe.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_grain.pl: Approximation: in the game it comes from beach iron sand (really mostly from river sands in Colombia and the Urals).
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroplatinic_ac: An orange liquid: platinum dissolved in aqua regia.

H2PtCl6 in water (glass bottle). Crafting: 2 placer platinum + 3 hydrochloric acid + 1 nitric acid (aqua regia; bottles come back) + 1 empty glass bottle → 1. Mixed with 2 ammonium chloride it gives a yellow precipitate. GHS: corrosive, respiratory sensitiser.

Platinum resists every single acid but dissolves in aqua regia, 3 parts hydrochloric to 1 part nitric. The nitric acid oxidises the platinum and chloride ions grab it into solution. The name ('royal water') comes from dissolving gold, the king of metals.
Repeated contact with platinum salts can cause a serious allergy (platinosis), so refineries take care not to breathe them in.
Approximation: evaporating the aqua regia, filtering and separating palladium and the other platinum metals are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonium_chloropl: A yellow powder that settles out of the platinum solution. Baking it gives platinum.
(NH4)2PtCl6. Crafting: 1 chloroplatinic acid solution + 2 ammonium chloride → 1 (the glass bottle comes back). Baked in a furnace it becomes platinum sponge.
H2PtCl6 + 2NH4Cl → (NH4)2PtCl6↓ + 2HCl. It hardly dissolves, so it sinks, while iron, copper and other metals stay in the liquid: this is where platinum is separated.
Heating breaks it down, roughly (NH4)2PtCl6 → Pt + 2NH4Cl + 2Cl2, leaving a porous, sponge-like platinum.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_sponge.n: A porous lump of platinum, like a sponge.
Left after baking the yellow precipitate in a furnace. Press 2 into a compact and forge it at white heat in a blast furnace to get a platinum ingot.
Its huge surface makes it a good catalyst: hydrogen meeting oxygen on it catches fire by itself (Döbereiner's lamp, 1823).
Platinum melts at about 1768 °C, beyond early-19th-century furnaces, so a way to consolidate the powder without melting was needed.
2 platinum sponge → 1 (crafting). Heated to white heat in a blast furnace, the grains bond (sintering) into a platinum ingot.

Around 1800 Wollaston pressed fine platinum powder with a screw press, heated it white-hot and hammered it, making workable platinum that nobody else could. This was the beginning of powder metallurgy.
Wollaston kept the method secret for life and made a fortune from platinum, discovering palladium and rhodium along the way.
Approximation: pressed at the crafting table instead of a screw press.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_ingot.no: A heavy, silvery-white metal that never rusts and resists acids.
Made by heating the platinum compact in a blast furnace (c:ingots/platinum). Becomes the anode in the hydrogen peroxide cell [2-19].
Platinum barely dissolves even where oxygen is produced in electrolysis, so it was essential for strongly oxidising electrolysis (persulfate, hydrogen peroxide).
From 1889 to 2019 the kilogram was defined by a cylinder of 90% platinum and 10% iridium (the International Prototype Kilogram).
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.note1: A clay furnace. Roasting iron ore with charcoal gives a lump of iron that never melts.
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.note2: Load iron ore (or iron sand) and charcoal, then keep pumping the bellows beside it to pass 1100 °C. Fire alone stops at about 800 °C. Heat the bloom red-hot in a furnace and hammer it with a hammerstone to get wrought iron (an iron ingot).
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.note3: Carbon monoxide from the burning charcoal takes the oxygen from the ore (Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2). At about 1200 °C iron (melting point 1538 °C) stays solid and forms a spongy lump full of slag.
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.note4: Iron smelting began around 1400–1200 BC. Anatolia and its surroundings are among the proposed places, but nothing is certain. Iron hammered free of slag is low in carbon and soft (wrought iron).
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.placeho: Approximation: temperatures and times are game values; vanilla raw iron is treated as hematite Fe2O3
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.note1: A spongy lump of iron from the bloomery.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.note2: Reheat it red-hot in a furnace, then hammer it with a hammerstone in the crafting grid to get wrought iron (an iron ingot). It can't be forged cold.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.note3: It is full of holes because it was reduced as a solid, without melting. Glassy slag (silicates) fills the gaps.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.note4: Smiths reheated the bloom red-hot and hammered and folded it again and again to squeeze the slag out. The 'kera' of Japanese tatara iron-making is also iron that never melted.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.placeh: Approximation: one reheating in a furnace
gui.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.need_ore: Add iron ore or iron sand
block.semiconductor-lab.blast_furnace_he: The lowest opening of a tall brick furnace. Molten iron flows out here.

Place it at the bottom middle of the front and build bricks around it, 3×3×4. The four sides of the 2nd layer are tuyeres; keep the inside empty. Put a water-powered bellows outside a tuyere for a steady blast. Opening the screen lights up missing spots.

A tall furnace with a strong, steady blast reaches about 1500 °C. Carbon dissolves into the iron and lowers its melting point to about 1150 °C, so the iron runs out as liquid (pig iron, about 4% carbon). Limestone turns the ore's earth into slag that separates from the iron.

China made pig iron in blast furnaces from about the 5th century BC and cast it in molds. Europe took it up around the 14th century. In 1709 Darby used coke instead of charcoal so forests no longer had to be cut (this furnace also runs on coke).
Approximation: temperatures, times and the limestone amount are game values; the lining is fired brick (refractory brick [3-12] comes with later furnaces)
block.semiconductor-lab.tuyere.note1: A fired clay pipe that blows the bellows' air into the furnace.
block.semiconductor-lab.tuyere.note2: Put them on the four sides of the blast furnace's 2nd layer. A bellows outside sends its air into the furnace.
block.semiconductor-lab.tuyere.note3: Right in front of the tuyere is the hottest place in the furnace. Charcoal burns hard there, and the carbon monoxide rises and takes the oxygen from the ore.
block.semiconductor-lab.tuyere.note4: Later big blast furnaces made tuyeres of copper cooled by flowing water, and preheated the blast (hot blast, 1828).
item.semiconductor-lab.pig_iron.note1: Iron that ran out of a blast furnace. Lots of carbon: hard but brittle.
item.semiconductor-lab.pig_iron.note2: Blow air through it in a converter and the carbon burns away, giving steel.
item.semiconductor-lab.pig_iron.note3: With about 4% carbon it melts about 400 °C below pure iron (1538 °C), which is why it flows out of the blast furnace as liquid. It cracks when hammered, so it is cast in molds.
item.semiconductor-lab.pig_iron.note4: The name comes from the sand molds: thin bars of iron branching off a main channel looked like piglets lined up at a sow.
item.semiconductor-lab.blast_furnace_sla: Stony waste that separates from the iron in a blast furnace.
Limestone and the ore's earth (silica) melt together into it. It is lighter than iron and floats on the molten metal.
CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3. Without slag, the earth would set inside and choke the furnace.
Today blast furnace slag is ground up for cement and used under roads.
item.semiconductor-lab.hot_iron_bloom.no: A bloom heated until it glows red. Now it can be hammered.
Put it in the crafting grid with a hammerstone to beat the slag out and get wrought iron (an iron ingot). The hammerstone comes back.
Above about 1000 °C the slag in the gaps softens. Hammering welds the iron grains together and squeezes the slag out. Wrought iron has under 0.1% carbon and is soft and tough.

Heating wrought iron packed in charcoal for a long time lets carbon soak into the surface (carburizing); quenching it in water then makes a blade. Wrought iron dates from the start of iron smelting, around 1400–1200 BC ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.hot_iron_bloom.pl: Approximation: heat once, hammer once (really heated and hammered again and again)
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_crucible.note: A crucible shaped from clay, not yet fired.
5 clay + refractory brick (crushed as grog). Fired in the blast furnace it becomes a fire-clay crucible.
Huntsman made his own crucibles from Stourbridge fire clay mixed with coke dust and ground old crucibles, kneaded by treading.
Mixing in already-fired clay (grog) reduces shrinking and cracking in the kiln, a basic trick of refractory making.
item.semiconductor-lab.clay_crucible.not: A clay pot that does not crack even when hot enough to melt iron.
A raw crucible fired in the blast furnace. Add 2 wrought iron and charcoal to make a crucible charge.
Iron melts at about 1500 C. Ordinary pottery softens before that, so heat-resistant fire clay was needed.
Real crucibles lasted about three heats, wearing each time the steel was poured, until they cracked.
item.semiconductor-lab.crucible_charge.n: A crucible filled with iron and charcoal and lidded. Melting it in the blast furnace makes steel.
Fire-clay crucible + 2 wrought iron (iron ingot) + charcoal. Melted in the blast furnace -> 2 crucible steel (the crucible breaks). An ordinary furnace is not hot enough.
Around 1740 the clockmaker Huntsman, wanting even steel for springs, found how to melt steel completely in a lidded crucible.
The lid keeps air out, so carbon does not burn away and mixes evenly into the molten iron. Indian wootz steel was also made by sealing iron with plant matter (carbon) in crucibles.
item.semiconductor-lab.crucible_charge.p: Approximation: the real charge was carburized blister steel melted over a coke fire (about 1550 C). Here wrought iron and charcoal go in together and the blast furnace melts them. The crucible breaks after one heat (really about three).
item.semiconductor-lab.crucible_steel.no: Fine steel with even carbon. Quenched, it becomes very hard.
Steel from melting a crucible charge (about 1% carbon). For clock springs, blades and precision parts (gauge blocks [8-05]).
Sheffield crucible steel, called 'cast steel', was the finest steel for blades and tools for over a century.
Earlier blister steel had more carbon at the surface than inside. Fully melted steel is equally hard wherever you cut it, an evenness that precision gauges depend on.
block.semiconductor-lab.stibnite_ore.not: An ore of long, needle-like silver-grey crystals. The source of antimony.
Sb2S3. Forms in the same hydrothermal vein band as galena (height -16 to 64). Mine with a stone pickaxe or better.
Metals and sulfur dissolved in hot underground water crystallized as it cooled in rock cracks (a hydrothermal vein).
Stibnite from the Ichinokawa mine in Ehime, Japan forms superb crystals tens of centimetres long, found in museums worldwide.
block.semiconductor-lab.stibnite_ore.pla: Approximation: generates at the same heights as galena (half as many).
item.semiconductor-lab.stibnite.note1: A mineral of antimony and sulfur. People long ago ground it up for eye make-up.
item.semiconductor-lab.stibnite.note2: Roast it in a furnace for antimony trioxide. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (swallowed, inhaled), hazardous to aquatic life.
item.semiconductor-lab.stibnite.note3: Roasted in air, the sulfur leaves as sulfur dioxide and the antimony becomes an oxide: 2Sb2S3 + 9O2 -> 2Sb2O3 + 6SO2.
item.semiconductor-lab.stibnite.note4: Since at least 3000 BC it was used in ancient Egypt and elsewhere for black eye shadow (kohl).
item.semiconductor-lab.stibnite.placehol: Approximation: the sulfur dioxide by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.antimony_trioxide: A white powder from roasting stibnite.
Roast stibnite in a furnace. Reduce it again in a furnace (with the fuel's carbon) for antimony. ⚠ GHS: carcinogenic (category 2).
Sb2O3 + 3C -> 2Sb + 3CO. The same two-step route as lead (galena -> lead oxide -> lead).
Today it is used in large amounts as a helper for flame retardants in plastics.
Approximation: reduced by the fuel's carbon.
item.semiconductor-lab.antimony.note1: A silvery, brittle metal that shatters when struck. It expands slightly as it solidifies.
item.semiconductor-lab.antimony.note2: Reduce antimony trioxide in a furnace. + chlorine -> antimony pentachloride (a catalyst for adding fluorine, [2-38]). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (inhaled), hazardous to aquatic life.
item.semiconductor-lab.antimony.note3: A group-15 metalloid (like nitrogen and phosphorus). A little in germanium or silicon leaves one spare electron: n-type.
item.semiconductor-lab.antimony.note4: Because it expands as it sets, type metal (lead + tin + antimony) fills the corners of the mould sharply (printing). It also hardens lead-acid battery plates. Biringuccio's Pirotechnia (1540) has a chapter on antimony; whether it describes taking the sulfur away with iron is not confirmed ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.antimony.placehol: Approximation: the iron route (Sb2S3 + 3Fe -> 2Sb + 3FeS) is not included; only roast then reduce.
block.semiconductor-lab.chromite_ore.not: A black ore deep in the deepslate. The raw material of chromium.
Found in deepslate (Y -64 to 0). Mine with an iron pickaxe or better for chromite.
Chromite forms in peridotite and serpentinite, rocks from deep in the Earth (the mantle). South Africa, Kazakhstan and India are major producers.
Minecraft has no peridotite or serpentinite, so deep deepslate stands in for them.
block.semiconductor-lab.chromite_ore.pla: Approximation: appears in deep deepslate instead of peridotite and serpentinite.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromite.note1: A heavy black ore full of chromium.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromite.note2: FeCr2O4. 2 + 2 sodium carbonate + quicklime make a roast charge. A furnace alone does not give chromium.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromite.note3: Chromium was found in 1797 by the Frenchman Vauquelin in a red Siberian mineral (crocoite). Its compounds come in many colors, so it was named after the Greek for color, chroma.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromite.note4: In chromite, iron and chromium are tightly bound to oxygen. Reducing it with carbon gives carbon-rich ferrochrome (for stainless steel); pure chromium is made by taking it apart chemically first.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromite_roast_ch: Chromite mixed with soda and lime, to be roasted hard in air.
2 chromite + 2 sodium carbonate + quicklime. Roasted in the blast furnace -> 2 sodium chromate.
Soda roasting: 4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 -> 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2. Oxygen from the air turns chromium hexavalent as a water-soluble salt. The lime keeps the charge from melting into a lump.
Washing the roast with water leaves yellow sodium chromate solution and a red iron-oxide residue. That residue (chromium slag) still held hexavalent chromium and caused pollution.
Approximation: the iron-oxide residue and the water leaching are skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_chromate.n: 2 from roasting the charge in the blast furnace. 2 + sulfuric acid + potassium carbonate make potassium dichromate. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing, acute toxicity, skin corrosion, respiratory and skin sensitization, carcinogenicity (category 1B), mutagenicity, reproductive toxicity, aquatic hazard. Handled only as an industrial material.
Hexavalent chromium compounds were widely used for plating, pigments, tanning and wood preserving, but breathing them can perforate the nasal septum and cause lung cancer.

Lesson: in 1975 it came to light in Tokyo and elsewhere that slag from a chromium chemicals plant had been used as landfill; soil contamination and lung cancer and nasal perforation among former workers became a public issue. Technology and regulations to avoid using and releasing hexavalent chromium followed.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromium_oxide.no: A green powder, also used as a paint pigment.
Potassium dichromate decomposed by heating in a furnace (4K2Cr2O7 -> 4K2CrO4 + 2Cr2O3 + 3O2). With 2 aluminium and a crucible it makes a thermite charge.
Trivalent chromium is far less toxic than hexavalent. It is used as a green pigment (chrome green) and as a polishing compound.
Going from hexavalent (orange, yellow) to trivalent (green) changes the color; old breath alcohol testers used this color change.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromium_oxide.pl: Approximation: the potassium chromate formed in the decomposition is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.thermite_charge.n: Chromium oxide and aluminium powder in a crucible. Once lit, aluminium takes the oxygen and molten chromium comes out.

Chromium oxide + 2 aluminium + fire-clay crucible. Lit in the blast furnace -> 2 chromium. ⚠ GHS: flammable solid (aluminium powder). Handled only as industrial reduction (metal making, rail welding).
In 1894-95 the German Goldschmidt devised the thermite process, making metals with the great heat released as aluminium binds oxygen. With no carbon involved, it gave carbon-free pure chromium.
Cr2O3 + 2Al -> 2Cr + Al2O3. The reaction heat reaches about 2000 C and needs no outside heating. It is still used to weld railway rails on site.
item.semiconductor-lab.thermite_charge.p: Approximation: really it only needs lighting, no furnace (here the blast furnace stands in for ignition). The alumina slag is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromium.note1: A shiny silvery metal, hard and rust-resistant.
item.semiconductor-lab.chromium.note2: 2 from lighting a thermite charge in the blast furnace. Evaporated onto a quartz plate it becomes the material of chrome masks [7-12].
item.semiconductor-lab.chromium.note3: A very thin oxide film forms on the surface and protects it (passivation). Added to iron it makes stainless steel, and with nickel, heating wire (nichrome).
item.semiconductor-lab.chromium.note4: IC masks are made by coating a quartz plate with about 0.1 um of chromium and etching it into the circuit pattern. Chromium blocks light well, resists scratches and lasts thousands of uses.
A yellowish, metallic-looking ore deep underground. The source of nickel.
(Fe,Ni)9S8. Forms deep in the overworld (height -60 to 0, in deepslate). Mine with an iron pickaxe or better.
As deep magma cooled, heavy iron-nickel sulfides sank and collected at the bottom (magmatic segregation).
Sudbury in Canada is one of the world's greatest nickel districts, in a basin made by a meteorite impact about 1.8 billion years ago.
Approximation: accompanying minerals (pyrrhotite, chalcopyrite) are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.pentlandite.note1: A mineral of nickel, iron and sulfur.
item.semiconductor-lab.pentlandite.note2: + sand -> matte charge. ⚠ GHS: carcinogenic (nickel sulfide dust, inhaled).
item.semiconductor-lab.pentlandite.note3: It holds about as much iron as nickel; removing the iron first is the key step.
item.semiconductor-lab.pentlandite.note4: Named after the Irish naturalist Pentland, who described it in 1856.
item.semiconductor-lab.matte_charge.note: Ore mixed with sand. When fired, the iron joins the sand as slag and separates.
Iron combines with oxygen and sand (SiO2) into slag (iron silicate), which floats. The heavy nickel sulfide sinks (the matte).
Copper smelting makes the same kind of 'matte'.
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel_matte.note: A lump of nickel sulfide with the iron removed.
Fire the matte charge in a furnace. Roast it again in a furnace for nickel oxide.
Mostly Ni3S2. Roasted in air, the sulfur leaves as sulfur dioxide and the nickel becomes an oxide.
Mond's refinery (1902, Clydach in Britain) refined matte shipped from Sudbury, Canada.
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel_matte.plac: Approximation: no copper; no sulfur dioxide produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel_oxide.note: A green powder. Reduced with hydrogen it turns back into nickel.
Roast nickel matte in a furnace. + a bag of hydrogen -> crude nickel. ⚠ GHS: carcinogenic (category 1A, inhaled), skin sensitizer.
German miners blamed a mischievous goblin ('Nickel') for an ore that looked like copper but gave none, hence the name. Cronstedt isolated nickel in 1751.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_nickel.note: Nickel still mixed with a little iron and copper. Purified by the Mond process.
Nickel oxide + hydrogen. + 4 bags of carbon monoxide -> nickel carbonyl.
