In the Mond process it is first reduced with hydrogen (water gas) at about 400 C.
This powder has a very active surface and combines readily with carbon monoxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_nickel.plac: Approximation: reduction temperature is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.carbon_monoxide_g: A gas with no colour or smell that is very harmful.

2 coke + a bag of oxygen make 2 (burned with little oxygen). Material for nickel carbonyl and the Reppe process. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (inhaled, category 3), flammable gas, reproductive toxicity, specific target organ toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
2C + O2 -> 2CO. It binds to haemoglobin in blood over 200 times more strongly than oxygen, so blood cannot carry oxygen.
Burning charcoal or coal in a closed room causes carbon monoxide poisoning; homes now have alarms for it.
Approximation: 1 bag = about 1 mol. The gas producer is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel_carbonyl_g: Nickel joined with carbon monoxide into a gas. Highly toxic. If you carry it, some may leak and make you feel ill.

Crude nickel + 4 bags of carbon monoxide (about 50 C). Decompose in a furnace (about 200 C) for nickel. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (inhaled, category 2), carcinogenic (category 1B), reproductive toxicity, flammable. Treated only as an industrial material.
Ni + 4CO -> Ni(CO)4 (about 50 C); Ni(CO)4 -> Ni + 4CO (about 200 C). Iron and copper do not become gases at these temperatures, so only nickel is taken out.

In 1890 Mond and his team found it while studying why nickel valves corroded in carbon monoxide. A metal turning into a gas was a great surprise. Because it is so toxic, plants keep it strictly away from air.
Approximation: the carbon monoxide released on decomposition is not recovered (really it is reused). Leaks do not use up the bag.
message.semiconductor-lab.nickel_carbony: Nickel carbonyl leaked. Headache and weakness (highly toxic)
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel.note1: A silvery-white metal that resists rust. Found in coins and stainless steel.
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel.note2: Decompose nickel carbonyl in a furnace (Mond process, very pure). + aluminium -> Raney nickel precursor (catalyst, [2-51]). ⚠ GHS: skin sensitizer, suspected carcinogen (category 2).
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel.note3: Like iron and cobalt, it sticks to magnets. It soaks up hydrogen readily, so it catalyzes reactions that add hydrogen (hydrogenation).
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel.note4: In 1897 Sabatier found that nickel catalyzes adding hydrogen to oils and unsaturated compounds (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1912). Margarine is made with this reaction.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_crystal.note: Quartz grown into a large clear crystal. A curious stone that makes electricity when squeezed.
A rare drop from quartz veins mined without silk touch. Cut it with a diamond saw for quartz blanks.

In 1880 the Curie brothers (Pierre and Jacques) found that squeezing quartz produces electric charge on its surface (piezoelectricity). Conversely, a voltage makes the crystal stretch or shrink slightly.
Brazil was the big source of natural quartz, and radio crystals ran short in World War II, which led to synthetic quartz [8-18].
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.note1: An iron plate with holes that get smaller step by step. Pull a metal rod through them in turn and it becomes a thin wire.
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.note2: Crafting: 3 iron ingots + 1 flint → 1 (the flint pierces the holes). Gold ingot + draw plate → 8 gold wire; copper ingot + draw plate → 8 copper wire. The plate comes back (not used up).
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.note3: Going through a hole, the metal gets as much longer as it gets thinner (the volume stays the same). Too big a step snaps it, so it is pulled through dozens of slightly smaller holes.
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.note4: Wire was pulled by hand from ancient times; in 14th-century Nuremberg water power took over (⚠️ the date is uncertain). Roebling's 1893 stranding machine twisted steel wires into suspension-bridge ropes.
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.placeh: Approximation: the graded holes are one plate and drawing is done at the crafting table. The tool is not used up.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_die.note1: A diamond with a tiny hole through it. It can draw very thin wire.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_die.note2: Crafting: 1 diamond + 1 iron ingot (mount) → 1. Gold wire + diamond die → 8 gold bonding wire. The die comes back.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_die.note3: Holes in an iron plate wear wider, but a diamond hole hardly wears, so even wire finer than a hair stays the same thickness.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_die.note4: Light-bulb tungsten wire and chip gold wire (about 25 µm) are drawn through diamond dies. ⚠️ When diamond dies became common is not yet checked.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_wire.note1: Gold wire drawn through a draw plate.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_wire.note2: Gold ingot + draw plate → 8. Drawn again through a diamond die it becomes fine gold bonding wire for chips.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_wire.note3: Gold is soft and extremely ductile: a gram can be drawn into kilometres of wire. It never rusts, so it suits electrical contacts.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_wire.note4: Hammered gold leaf gets as thin as about 0.1 µm.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_bonding_wire: Gold wire a third as thick as a hair. It connects a chip to the outside leads.
Gold wire + diamond die → 8 (about 25 µm across). The wire bonder [9-33] joins chip pads to header leads with it (one wire per pad).
Gold does not rust and sticks to aluminium pads under heat and pressure, so it was chosen to wire up chips.
Cheaper copper wire is common today, but it is harder to bond (copper oxidises and is harder).
Approximation: thickness is not modelled. One wire = one pad.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_wire.note1: Copper wire drawn through a draw plate. The core of electric cables.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_wire.note2: Copper ingot + draw plate → 8. Few uses yet (cable cores, submarine cable [15-03]).
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_wire.note3: Copper conducts electricity second only to silver and is cheap and ductile, so almost all wiring is copper.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_wire.note4: Copper wire is made by pulling a thick rod through small holes dozens of times.
